title: Ershad seizes power
detail: Army chief Hussain Muhammad Ershad took power through a military coup and began a long period of authoritarian rule.

title: Student resistance becomes the earliest organized front
detail: Students emerged as some of the first consistent opponents of military rule, keeping street resistance alive when democratic space was narrow.

title: Nur Hossain becomes a martyr-symbol
detail: Activist Nur Hossain was shot dead during an anti-Ershad blockade in Dhaka. The slogan painted on his body became one of the movement's most enduring democratic cries.

title: Boycotted election deepens the legitimacy crisis
detail: Major opposition parties rejected the 1988 parliamentary election, intensifying the regime's political isolation.

title: The anti-Ershad movement becomes fully national
detail: By 1990, hartals, blockades, campus strikes, and demonstrations had intensified, with students, parties, and professionals acting in greater coordination.

title: The three alliances agree on a joint formula
detail: The main opposition alliances issued a combined declaration on democratic transition, creating a decisive common front against the regime.

title: Emergency is declared
detail: The regime imposed emergency rule and suspended fundamental rights, but the move failed to halt the uprising.

title: Professional groups and citizens join the final push
detail: Teachers, doctors, lawyers, journalists, artists, and broad sections of the public joined the final wave of pressure.

title: Ershad resigns and power shifts to Shahabuddin Ahmed
detail: Under intense public pressure, Ershad stepped down and power passed to Chief Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed as head of a neutral caretaker arrangement.

title: Democratic transition is completed
detail: A competitive election was held under the caretaker government, and later in 1991 the parliamentary system was restored through the Twelfth Amendment.
